problem_statement: Fixed-block rolling estimators are widely used in practice for volatility functionals and related statistical targets, but their efficiency theory is underdeveloped when block size remains finite. problem_core: The fundamental bottleneck is the absence of a general fixed-block minimum-variance theory for unbiased rolling estimators when overlap-induced covariance makes classical UMVU-based constructions suboptimal.
problem_type_fine: fixed-block estimator efficiency
failure_mode_or_limitation: classical UMVU and diverging-block efficiency theory fail to characterize or attain the minimum variance of unbiased estimators at fixed block size because covariance among overlapping blocks is ignored
intervention_or_solution: development of BUMVU estimation theory based on covariance kernels, with necessary and sufficient optimality conditions and constructive fixed-m estimators for variance, quarticity, and drift-robust integrated variance
mechanism_or_rationale: The proposed theory treats a block estimator's covariance kernel as the key object controlling overlap-induced covariance across rolling blocks. problem_statement: Vehicle tyre and aerodynamic resistances strongly affect road-vehicle energy use and CO2 emissions, but standard certification methods determine these resistances using specialized coast-down or constant-speed procedures that are costly, infrastructure-intensive, and partly disconnected from actual on-road operating conditions. problem_statement: Cooperative multi-robot systems for flexible manufacturing are limited by kinematic overdetermination, synchronization demands, and control architectures that do not scale or adapt well, especially when mobile robots are involved. hypothesis: Applying a virtual-robot-model-based control framework with modified admittance control to cooperative multi-robot systems addresses kinematic overdetermination because the VRM provides a centralized motion reference without centralized feedback, while compliant orientation-passive robot behavior absorbs asynchronous motion errors as bounded virtual spring deflection, thereby improving scalability, adaptability, and safe cooperative object handling/transport.

intervention_or_solution: A scalable cooperative multi-robot control framework combining a Virtual Robot Model for centralized motion-sequence specification with decentralized execution and a modified admittance controller that makes TCP orientation passive like a virtual ball joint.
mechanism_or_rationale: The VRM serves as a common kinematic reference so existing single-robot motion sequences can be reused without centralized feedback control or robot-specific reprogramming, keeping communication and computation largely independent of robot count. The modified admittance controller converts pose errors from asynchronous motion into bounded compliant displacements and virtual spring tension rather than aggressive error correction, which suppresses jamming-induced force amplification. By removing active orientation resistance at the TCP, the controller effectively reduces orientation-related degrees of freedom and thus mitigates kinematic overdetermination, allowing object orientation to be set passively by the cooperative geometry.

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Flexible manufacturing requires assembly and handling systems that can scale output and adapt to changing products, but single stationary robots are constrained by fixed range, payload, and precision. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Using multiple robots can increase throughput, yet cooperative manipulation of one shared object introduces extra robot degrees of freedom without increasing the object's six degrees of freedom, creating kinematic overdetermination. [End Step 2]

[End Step 7]

problem_statement: Heat extraction by superfluid helium in superconducting magnet cooling is strongly hindered in narrow, high-aspect-ratio gaps such as those created by insulation tapes and collar spacings. intervention_or_solution: Experimental investigation using clamped heat fluxes in pressurized superfluid helium rectangular channels of two thicknesses (0.2 mm and 0.5 mm) to isolate the effect of heat flux and confinement on λ-front and boiling-front propagation
mechanism_or_rationale: When heat flux exceeds the λ-threshold in confined He II, He II first transforms to He I, but sufficiently large heat loads in narrow channels also trigger boiling because the small coolant volume limits convective and boiling heat removal. As vapour regions coalesce into a homogeneous film at the heater, the low thermal conductivity of vapour sharply increases the local temperature gradient and cuts the direct thermal link between the heater and He II, slowing or shortening λ-front propagation and reducing the longitudinal extent of the He I region. Channel thickness changes the confinement number and thus the ease of vapour/He I expansion, which determines whether a three-zone double-front behavior appears or whether λ-front motion is more weakly limited by confinement.
target_property: λ-front speed and multiphase phase-distribution/thermal transport behavior in confined He II
claimed_outcome: Identification of confinement- and heat-flux-dependent multiphase regimes, including double-front propagation and the role of vapour-film growth in limiting λ-front motion, providing a mechanistic basis for predicting thermal barriers in superconducting-magnet cooling gaps

keywords_compact: He II | lambda transition | film boiling | confinement | double front | quench cooling | thermal barrier
reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Superfluid helium is normally an exceptional coolant for superconducting magnets, but in real magnet assemblies the helium is confined in narrow gaps created by insulation tapes and collars, so the effective heat-removal pathway is geometrically restricted. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Under high heat dissipation, these confined gaps can no longer be described by simple He II conduction alone because the applied heat flux can exceed the threshold for the He II→He I λ-transition and may also induce boiling. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] Once vapour appears near the heater, the very low thermal conductivity of helium vapour compared with liquid phases creates an insulating layer that increases the local temperature gradient and changes the propagation of thermal and phase fronts. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] Therefore, the dominant unresolved issue is not merely whether transition occurs, but how heat flux magnitude and channel confinement jointly determine the coupled propagation of the λ-front and boiling front. [End Step 4]
[Begin Step 5] The study addresses this by using controlled clamped-flux experiments in two rectangular channels of different thicknesses, allowing the confinement level to be changed while directly tracking temperatures along the channel during transients. [End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] The measurements show that at lower-to-moderate heat fluxes the λ-front initially accelerates with heat flux, but as vapour-film boiling develops, the λ-front slows, shortens, or becomes governed by vapour expansion; this produces distinct multiphase regimes and, in the thinner channel, a three-zone behavior with a speed maximum. [End Step 6]
[Begin Step 7] From these observations, the paper concludes that vapour-film growth is the key mechanism controlling thermal-barrier formation in confined He II and that geometric confinement sets the relative extent of He II, He I, and vapour, thereby determining cooling performance and quench-relevant heat extraction in superconducting-magnet gaps. [End Step 7]

hypothesis: Applying a unified layered control architecture that integrates SDN, IoT, Fog computing, and NFV to nano-networks addresses the limited computation, energy, and protocol-handling capability of nano-devices because higher network layers can externalize decision-making, coordination, and service logic, thereby improving controllability, functionality, and manageability of large-scale nano-network operation.

By decoupling simple device-level actions from complex network decision-making, the framework enables lightweight nano-devices to execute basic functions while SDN/NFV/IoT/Fog layers manage addressing, coordination, localization, feedback handling, and service control. This hierarchical abstraction is intended to reduce protocol burden on nano-machines and enable organized large-scale operation.

problem_statement: Hierarchically porous spinel MgMn2O4 is a promising cathode for rechargeable magnesium batteries because its nanoscale size and high surface area facilitate Mg2+ insertion/extraction, but its strongly hydrophilic surface adsorbs water and causes severe aggregation in NMP-based slurry processing. This aggregation and the associated poor contact/current collection, together with cathode-side charging side reactions, hinder fabrication of uniform high-active-material cathodes and reduce coulombic efficiency and full-cell performance.
hypothesis: Applying phenylphosphonate surface functionalisation to structured MgMn2O4 cathodes addresses slurry aggregation and charging-side parasitic reactions because covalently anchored phosphonate groups passivate reactive oxide surface sites while phenyl groups render the surface hydrophobic and increase affinity to CNT conductive additives, thereby improving slurry/coating homogeneity, interfacial stability, coulombic efficiency, and practical full-cell discharge performance.
problem_core: The fundamental bottleneck is that high-surface-area hydrophilic MgMn2O4 cathodes are difficult to process into uniform non-aqueous slurry-coated electrodes and suffer surface-driven charging side reactions, undermining practical RMB performance.
problem_type_fine: slurry aggregation and cathode-side side reactions
failure_mode_or_limitation: Hydrophilic water-adsorbing MgMn2O4 aggregates in NMP slurries and exposes reactive surface sites that promote oxidative side reactions during charging.
intervention_or_solution: Surface functionalisation of structured MgMn2O4 with phenylphosphonate groups before preparing CNT/PVDF/NMP slurry-coated cathodes.
mechanism_or_rationale: Phenylphosphonate groups form covalent P–O–(Mn,Mg) bonds on the MgMn2O4 surface, creating a thin surface layer that reduces water adsorption and passivates catalytically active sites responsible for electrolyte oxidation during charging. The surface-bound phenyl groups make the oxide more hydrophobic, suppressing aggregation in NMP-based slurries, and also enhance affinity to CNTs through π interactions, which improves conductive contact and current collection. Together these changes increase cathode homogeneity and interfacial stability without substantially blocking Mg2+ insertion/extraction, so discharge capacity is retained while parasitic charge loss is reduced.
target_property: slurry homogeneity and cathode interfacial stability
claimed_outcome: Uniform high-active-material slurry-coated cathodes with improved CNT contact, suppressed charging side reactions, higher coulombic efficiency, and an initial full-cell discharge capacity of about 100 mA h g−1 at 25 °C.
novelty_axis: new surface chemistry for practical cathode processing

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Structured MgMn2O4 is attractive for RMB cathodes because its small particle size, high surface area, and hierarchical pores shorten Mg2+ diffusion paths and improve Mg2+ insertion/extraction. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] The same high-surface-area oxide surface is strongly hydrophilic and adsorbs water, so in non-aqueous NMP slurry processing the particles form macroscopic aggregates instead of a uniform dispersion. [End Step 2]

[End Step 6]

problem_statement: Transfer learning by standard fine-tuning preserves the full parameter count and computational structure of the pre-trained source model even when the target task is much simpler, making deployment inefficient for storage- or latency-constrained settings. Existing adapters reduce per-task trainable parameters but often add computational overhead or do not improve inference efficiency, while fine-pruning still requires comparatively many learned task-specific weights under aggressive compression.
hypothesis: Applying structured-pruning-compatible fusible adapters, specifically Structured Pruning Adapters such as SPLoRA/SPPaRA, to pre-trained vision networks addresses the high per-task parameter and pruning fragility of fine-tuning because the adapters are anchored to frozen source weights and are pruned jointly with network channels, thereby preserving accuracy under aggressive structured pruning while greatly reducing learned parameter count and retaining inference efficiency.
problem_core: The paper aims to overcome the inability of conventional fine-tuning or conventional adapters to simultaneously achieve low per-task parameter count, maintained inference efficiency, and strong accuracy under aggressive structured pruning in transfer learning.
problem_type_fine: high per-task parameter count under aggressive structured pruning
component: pre-trained neural network layers under structured channel pruning
failure_mode_or_limitation: Fine-tuning with pruning learns too many task-specific weights and loses accuracy sharply at low model densities, while standard adapters often add compute rather than reducing it.
intervention_or_solution: Structured Pruning Adapters (SPAs), especially Structured Pruning Low-rank Adapters (SPLoRA) and Structure Pruning Parallel Residual Adapters (SPPaRA), fused with frozen source weights and jointly subjected to structured channel pruning.
mechanism_or_rationale: The proposed adapters are fusible parallel modules attached to frozen source weights, so after adaptation they can be merged into the original layer and inherit the same inference-time efficiency as structured pruning. Because pruning masks act on both source channels and adapter channels, the learned adapter parameter count scales with retained in/out channels rather than the full dense layer. The adapter remains anchored to the pre-trained source model, which the authors argue reduces catastrophic forgetting during iterative pruning and makes performance more robust when sparsity becomes aggressive.
target_property: learned parameter count per task and accuracy retention at low model density
claimed_outcome: Massively reduced per-task learned parameters with competitive or superior predictive accuracy relative to fine-pruning, especially for highly pruned models, while preserving the computational benefits of structured pruning.

keywords_compact: SPLoRA | SPPaRA | structured pruning | adapters | fine-pruning | transfer learning | iterative pruning
reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] In transfer learning, standard fine-tuning adapts a large pre-trained model to a simpler target task but keeps the full model size and computational profile, which is inefficient for edge, multi-task, or storage-limited deployment. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Fine-pruning can compress models through structured pruning, but task-specific learned weights can still remain substantial, and predictive accuracy degrades markedly when pruning becomes aggressive. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] Conventional adapters lower trainable parameter count for task specialization, yet many adapter designs increase or at best preserve inference complexity, so they do not fully solve efficiency requirements. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] A suitable design criterion is therefore an adapter that is both fusible into the base weights and compatible with structured channel pruning, so that no extra inference path remains after deployment and pruning can remove entire computational units. [End Step 4]
[Begin Step 5] The proposed SPAs implement this by adding low-rank or residual parallel adapter weights to frozen source layers and then applying the same structured channel masks to both source and adapter parameters, causing the learned parameter budget to shrink with retained channels. [End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] Because the adapter updates stay anchored to the original pre-trained weights instead of replacing them outright, iterative pruning is argued to induce less catastrophic forgetting, yielding better accuracy retention at low density while using far fewer task-specific parameters than fine-pruning. [End Step 6]

problem_statement: In lithium-ion full cells, the anode-to-cathode capacity ratio (N:P ratio) strongly affects performance, energy density, and safety, but its effect is entangled with correlated electrode properties such as coating weight, thickness, and areal capacity. hypothesis: Applying a design-of-experiments plus explainable machine-learning framework to graphite/NMC lithium-ion coin cells addresses the difficulty of disentangling N:P-ratio effects from correlated electrode variables because the approach jointly samples the multivariable design space and quantifies feature interactions and importance, thereby improving mechanistic understanding and prediction of rated capacity and gravimetric-capacity trends.
problem_core: The fundamental bottleneck is the inability to systematically quantify the isolated and relative impact of N:P ratio on Li-ion cell performance when electrode thickness, mass loading, and areal capacity covary.
problem_type_fine: confounded N:P-ratio impact analysis
failure_mode_or_limitation: masked dependence of cell performance on N:P ratio due to correlated electrode structural and loading variables
intervention_or_solution: purposeful design of experiments combined with Random Forest modeling and explainable machine-learning analysis (ALE, SHAP, and linear correlation) on graphite/NMC coin cells
mechanism_or_rationale: The DoE varies N:P ratio and cathode areal capacity across controlled breakpoints so that the effects of correlated manufacturing variables can be separated more systematically than with one-factor-at-a-time experiments. The Random Forest model captures nonlinear dependencies between electrode features and electrochemical responses, while ALE and SHAP reveal how N:P ratio contributes relative to cathode/anode mass and thickness. This exposes when N:P effects are weak, linear, or nonlinear and links performance changes at high C-rate to transitions toward mass-transport limitation in thicker cathodes.
target_property: quantifiable dependence of cell capacity and gravimetric capacity on N:P ratio and related electrode features
claimed_outcome: more systematic identification of the relative importance and nonlinear influence of N:P ratio, enabling improved prediction and optimization of Li-ion rated performance and gravimetric capacity

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] In Li-ion cells, electrode balancing via N:P ratio influences safety, energy density, and rate behavior, but N:P is inherently coupled to electrode mass loading, thickness, and areal capacity. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Because these variables covary during electrode manufacturing, visual inspection or one-factor-at-a-time experiments cannot reliably isolate whether observed performance changes arise from N:P ratio itself or from masking structural factors. [End Step 2]

problem_statement: Sustainable energy innovation uptake in the EU is limited not only by technical deployment barriers but by incomplete public acceptance, which includes both citizen adoption of technologies and support for technological and economic policy measures. reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Large-scale decarbonization depends on citizens both adopting sustainable energy technologies and supporting the policies that enable them; without acceptance, deployment and reform can stall. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Existing studies provide incomplete guidance because they often analyze only one manifestation of acceptance, focus on either technological or economic innovations alone, and frequently use adoption intention rather than actual adoption. [End Step 2]

problem_statement: Amide molybdate can deliver very low friction when used with ZDDP and fatty amine, but its practical optimization is limited by an incomplete understanding of how it decomposes under tribological contact to form the active lubricating phase. failure_mode_or_limitation: insufficient formation of crystalline MoS2 and persistence of amorphous MoS3 under mild tribological conditions
intervention_or_solution: Use a ternary lubricant additive formulation of amide molybdate with ZDDP and fatty triamine, and operate under higher temperature/pressure tribological conditions to promote conversion in the tribofilm.
mechanism_or_rationale: Amide molybdate is an oxidic Mo precursor that reacts with sulfur supplied by ZDDP to form sulfur-rich molybdenum sulfide species. Raman mapping indicates that an amorphous MoS3-like phase forms first and is progressively converted by friction-induced thermal and mechanical energy into MoS2, with more severe local conditions increasing MoS2 abundance and crystallinity. As the tribofilm becomes richer in MoS2, the lubricious low-shear phase dominates the contact and friction decreases.

claimed_outcome: lower friction coefficient and ultralow-friction tribofilm formation under severe conditions
novelty_axis: new mechanistic insight into tribofilm intermediate chemistry

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] The practical goal is to obtain stable ultralow friction from molybdenum-based lubricant additives, but this requires knowing how the active low-shear MoS2 phase forms in the sliding contact. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Unlike MoDTC, amide molybdate is an oxidic sulfur-free Mo precursor, so its conversion to MoS2 must occur through reactions with sulfur-containing co-additives such as ZDDP and may involve distinct intermediates. [End Step 2]

problem_statement: LiTFSI is a highly useful lithium salt for liquid and polymer electrolytes, but its chemical inertness makes it difficult to functionalize for polymer conjugation or single-ion conductor design. battery_system: lithium battery electrolyte systems including solid-state polymer electrolytes, lithium-sulfur, and lithium-air batteries
failure_mode_or_limitation: TFSI is chemically difficult to functionalize, and conventional substitutions often increase anion basicity and ion pairing while reducing oxidative and chemical stability, hindering use in tailored and single-ion-conducting electrolytes.
intervention_or_solution: Design and synthesis of Fluorinated Aryl Sulfonimide Tagged (FAST) salts based on perfluoroarylsulfonimide scaffolds functionalized through successive SNAr reactions with alkoxide and/or piperidine substituents.
mechanism_or_rationale: The perfluoroaryl sulfonimide framework maintains a strongly electron-deficient anion core while introducing chemically addressable positions for modular substitution. By varying substituent identity and pattern, the electron density and Lewis basicity of the anion are tuned, which changes oxidative susceptibility, nucleophilic stability toward superoxide/peroxide, and cation-anion association strength that controls ion dissociation and conductivity. Steric bulk and electron withdrawal together can preserve TFSI-like stability while still enabling functionalization, as illustrated by trisubstituted FAST salts such as A-ONeop3F2.
target_property: electrochemical oxidative stability, chemical stability, Lewis basicity/ion-pair association, and ionic conductivity of the electrolyte salt
claimed_outcome: Functionally tunable TFSI alternatives were obtained that preserve much of TFSI's advantageous stability while offering adjustable solubility and ion association, with selected FAST salts showing promising oxidative stability, negligible chemical degradation, and reasonable conductivity for electrolyte applications.

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Advanced lithium battery electrolytes, especially solid polymer electrolytes and beyond-LIB chemistries, require salts with high stability, adequate conductivity, and in some cases chemical functionality for polymer integration or single-ion transport. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] LiTFSI already offers excellent solubility and electrochemical/chemical stability, but its anion is chemically inert and therefore difficult to derivatize for conjugation to polymers or other substrates. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] Simple replacement of TFSI trifluoromethyl groups with more conventional phenyl or alkyl substituents tends to make the anion more electron rich, which is expected to lower oxidative stability and strengthen Li+/Na+ association, compromising electrolyte performance. [End Step 3]

[End Step 7]

intervention_or_solution: all-atom molecular dynamics simulation framework for polymer and polyelectrolyte brushes, explicitly modeling brush atoms, water molecules, and counterions
mechanism_or_rationale: Explicit all-atom MD retains individual atomic interactions that are averaged out in coarse-grained models and often inaccessible experimentally, allowing direct analysis of solvation shells, water hydrogen-bond networks, ion condensation/bridging, mobility, and brush conformational response. reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Polymer and polyelectrolyte brushes are widely used because their interfacial properties respond strongly to environmental conditions, but their performance depends on microscopic interactions within the brush layer. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Existing theories, experiments, and coarse-grained simulations can describe macroscopic quantities such as brush height or swelling, yet they cannot fully resolve atomistic solvent structure, ion binding, counterion-mediated bridging, and water hydrogen-bonding behavior inside the brush. problem_statement: Hosts capable of strongly recognizing large nonspherical anions are rare, and existing designs often lack straightforward synthetic tunability, so changing affinity typically requires redesigning the whole host scaffold. problem_statement: Electrical double layer capacitors require carbon electrodes with optimized pore architecture to simultaneously deliver high capacitance, fast ion transport, and high energy/power density. mechanism_or_rationale: ZnCl2 activation converts low-porosity hydrochar into a carbon with very high micropore surface area and some small mesopores. problem_statement: Super-Nernstian proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) has rarely been observed and, prior to this work, had not been demonstrated in an all-organic redox polymer. intervention_or_solution: Use of a multiredox phenazine-substituted ladder polymer (BBL-P) with carbonyl and imine redox sites of different pKa values, electrochemically n-doped in acidic aqueous electrolyte.
mechanism_or_rationale: The polymer backbone contains multiple protonatable redox centers with a pKa gradient, so reduction at one site increases electron density delocalized onto other imine sites and raises their basicity. reasoning_process:

problem_statement: Rice husk is an abundant biomass precursor for porous carbon adsorbents, but its high ash content and the poor pore structure produced by conventional deashing/carbonization routes limit its effectiveness for CO2 capture from flue gas. problem_statement: Pure boron phosphide monolayers have physical properties that may be insufficiently optimized for device use, particularly a relatively small band gap compared with what is desirable for nanoelectromechanical applications. problem_statement: Robots operating in unfamiliar environments must plan and act despite incomplete maps, uncertain sensing and action outcomes, and missing knowledge about relevant objects or rooms. These limitations make object search and other epistemic tasks brittle, and conventional planning struggles to handle open worlds, explain unexpected task failure, and verify explanations in a unified way.
hypothesis: Applying a three-layer instance-default-diagnostic knowledge organization with probabilistically weighted assumptive actions and switching deterministic/POMDP planning to robot task planning addresses open-world uncertainty and failure explanation because layered knowledge supports inference over current state, default commonsense, and diagnostic hypotheses, while assumptions instantiate likely missing facts and explanation candidates, thereby improving belief-guided planning, failure explanation, and verification outcomes.
problem_core: The fundamental bottleneck is how to let a robot plan, replan, and explain failures when the world model is incomplete and uncertain rather than closed and fully known.
problem_type_fine: planning under uncertainty in open worlds
component: robot knowledge representation and task planner
failure_mode_or_limitation: inability of standard planning to handle incomplete world models, uncertain observations, and unexpected task failures with explanation and verification
intervention_or_solution: Three-layer IDD knowledge schema (instance, default, diagnostic) combined with probabilistic assumptive actions, joint relational-map/default-knowledge inference, and a continual switching planner that combines deterministic planning with POMDP solving
mechanism_or_rationale: The framework couples current instance knowledge with probabilistic default knowledge so the robot can infer likely unseen rooms, objects, and relations and use these as generative assumptions during planning. mechanism_or_rationale: Dispersing metals as isolated atoms exposes nearly all metal atoms as catalytic centers, increasing active-site density per metal loading relative to nanoparticles with buried atoms. reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] OER is essential for water splitting and related electrochemical energy technologies, but it is intrinsically slow because it involves a demanding four-electron proton-coupled oxidation pathway with difficult O-H bond breaking and O-O bond formation steps. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Conventional nanoparticle or bulk catalysts are limited because many metal atoms are buried and inaccessible, some systems depend on scarce noble metals, and catalyst particles can aggregate, corrode, or deactivate during operation. [End Step 2]

problem_statement: Silicon solar modules are designed primarily for cost, efficiency, and reliability rather than end-of-life recovery, creating major barriers to circularity when large waste volumes emerge. problem_statement: Physics-based electrochemical-thermal models for lithium-ion batteries are needed for battery management, thermal management, and multi-cell stack analysis, but full pseudo-2D models are too computationally expensive for real-time or large-scale simulations. mechanism_or_rationale: Changing the urea/glycerol ratio alters the solubility of small counterions in the DES and the solvation environment of surfactant headgroups at the micelle shell. problem_statement: Rechargeable metal–iodine batteries are promising because iodine redox chemistry involves relatively few intermediates and can offer high reversibility, safety, and low cost. Reducing felt thickness decreases the through-thickness potential nonuniformity, allowing more uniform nucleation and coating coverage across the porous structure.

problem_statement: Auditory systems must classify behaviorally relevant vocalizations despite large within- and between-producer variability in their spectrotemporal structure. intervention_or_solution: Greedy-search extraction and detection of a small set of maximally informative mid-level cochleagram features (MIFs) with log-likelihood-weighted evidence integration.
mechanism_or_rationale: Intermediate-length, intermediate-complexity spectrotemporal features capture call substructures that are sufficiently conserved across exemplars of the same call type while avoiding the over-specificity of whole-call templates and the under-informativeness of very small fragments. Greedy search removes redundant features and retains those that add mutual information, so thresholded detections of multiple MIFs can be combined into a robust evidence signal that separates call categories despite production variability.

claimed_outcome: High-accuracy, production-invariant call classification using only a small number of features, with tuning predictions that resemble observed auditory cortical responses and generalization to caller identification and other species.

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Vocalizations from the same category vary substantially across individuals and productions, while different call categories overlap in long-term spectral content, so category identity cannot be read out reliably from simple spectral summaries or a single exemplar template. [Begin Step 2] Successful categorization therefore requires a representation that is simultaneously selective to distinguishing spectrotemporal structure and tolerant to within-category variability. [End Step 2]

mechanism_or_rationale: The finned heat-pipe CHX reduces total cold-side resistance through two coupled effects: near-isothermal internal heat transport by evaporation/condensation inside the pipes and enhanced external convection from an enlarged finned surface. [Begin Step 1] Geothermal TEGs are attractive for remote and harsh environments because they can generate electricity without moving parts, but their low efficiency makes preservation of the module temperature difference critical for useful power production. [End Step 1]

mechanism_or_rationale: The Al2O3 high-k dielectric increases gate capacitance relative to SiO2, enabling stronger channel charge modulation and lower subthreshold swing at low driving voltage. The HfO2 buffer prevents Al cations from diffusing from Al2O3 into the IZO channel and, at the interface, Hf acts as a carrier suppressor by forming strong Hf-O bonds that reduce oxygen-vacancy generation. Together these effects lower total trap density in the channel and at the channel-insulator interface, which improves switching characteristics and gate-bias stability.
target_property: gate capacitance and total trap density at the channel-insulator interface
claimed_outcome: improved switching characteristics, higher on-off ratio and mobility, reduced threshold-voltage shift under bias stress, and better low-power electrical performance

[Begin Step 2] Using high-k dielectrics instead of thick SiO2 can increase gate capacitance, so for a given gate bias more electrons can be accumulated and the transistor can be switched more effectively at low voltage. [End Step 2]

[End Step 6]

problem_statement: Recovering manganese from sulphide tailings is limited by the compositional complexity of the tailings and by drawbacks of conventional acid leaching routes. intervention_or_solution: Dilute HCl leaching of the sulphide tailings under optimized conditions (5% HCl, liquid-to-solid ratio 5, 90 min, 50 °C), followed by selective Mn precipitation from the pregnant leach solution using 0.1 M NH4OH at pH 9.8 and 48 °C.
mechanism_or_rationale: Dilute HCl selectively dissolves Mn-bearing rhodochrosite from the tailings while avoiding the CaSO4·2H2O gypsum paste formation associated with H2SO4 and avoiding nitrate-based harmful Fe(NO3)3 formation. The leaching proceeds via MnCO3 proton dissolution, and under optimized mild conditions Mn recovery remains high while Fe dissolution is minimized. Subsequent pH- and temperature-controlled NH4OH addition exploits differential metal hydroxide/oxide precipitation behavior so Mn precipitates preferentially as Mn oxide at around pH 9.8, yielding a high-purity Mn product.
target_property: Mn leaching selectivity and Mn product purity
claimed_outcome: High Mn recovery from sulphide tailings with limited Fe co-leaching and subsequent production of high-purity Mn oxide using dilute reagents, improving process sustainability and economic viability.

[Begin Step 2] Existing hydrometallurgical options are ill-suited to these tailings because H2SO4 reacts with Ca to form thick gypsum paste and HNO3-based leaching can require high acid dosage and generate environmentally harmful Fe(NO3)3 in Fe-sulphide-bearing materials. [End Step 2]

problem_statement: Dynamic decentralized multi-energy system (D-MES) planning is poorly served by existing design tools because most models are single-stage, myopic across years, spatially aggregated, or unable to account for technology evolution and end-of-horizon bias. This limits accurate long-term investment timing, siting, and sizing for interconnected district-scale energy systems, which matters for minimizing lifetime cost and CO2 emissions in real urban developments.
hypothesis: Applying the MANGO multi-stage MILP framework to decentralized multi-energy system design addresses myopic and biased long-term planning because it explicitly co-optimizes what, where, and when to invest across multiple years and locations while tracking technology-specific aging, future performance improvements, and salvage value, thereby improving long-term design optimality in terms of total system cost, CO2 emissions, and planning realism.
problem_core: The paper seeks to overcome the lack of a rigorous optimization framework for long-term, flexible, multi-location D-MES planning that captures evolving techno-economic conditions without myopic decisions or end-of-horizon distortion.

component: system-level design and operation planning framework
failure_mode_or_limitation: single-stage or sequentially myopic planning, omission of technological evolution, inability to optimize interconnected multi-location systems, and end-of-horizon bias in long-term investment decisions
intervention_or_solution: MANGO, a multi-year mixed-integer linear programming model for optimal multi-stage design of interconnected D-MES with flexible investment stages, separate tracking of each technology installation, dynamic techno-economic inputs, degradation modeling, and salvage-value treatment of end-of-horizon effects
mechanism_or_rationale: The model introduces explicit temporal, spatial, and technology-installation dimensions so that investment timing, location, capacity, and operation are optimized jointly over the full planning horizon rather than stage-by-stage independently. By tracking each installed unit separately, MANGO can represent differing efficiencies, degradation histories, and future technology improvements, which changes dispatch and replacement choices. Including salvage value credits mitigates the artificial penalization of late-horizon investments, enabling more faithful long-term cost and emissions optimization.
target_property: long-term design optimality and fidelity of investment timing/siting/sizing decisions
claimed_outcome: more accurate and flexible multi-stage D-MES plans with improved economic and environmental performance, reduced technological complexity through interconnections, and richer planning insight for district-scale energy system developers
novelty_axis: new optimization framework for dynamic multi-stage multi-location D-MES design

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Real D-MES projects evolve over decades, with changing loads, prices, technology performance, and phased district development, so static single-stage planning assumptions are structurally mismatched to the actual planning problem. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Existing single-stage or sequential year-by-year methods optimize each stage independently or aggregate the system too coarsely, which prevents them from valuing deferred investments, coordinated replacements, and cross-location sharing. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] Additional inaccuracies arise when all installations of the same technology are aggregated, because the model then cannot distinguish units installed in different years that have different costs, efficiencies, and degradation states. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] Long-term models also suffer from finite-horizon distortion, where late investments appear unattractive because their costs are fully counted but the remaining useful life beyond the horizon is not. [End Step 4]

[Begin Step 6] This structure causally improves planning fidelity because the optimizer can exploit future technology cost reductions and efficiency gains, account for degradation and replacement, dispatch newer versus older assets differently, and offset end-horizon bias through salvage values. [End Step 6]
[Begin Step 7] As a result, the framework is expected and shown in the case study to generate more realistic long-term plans and reveal benefits such as lower costs and emissions with interconnections, smoother and less complex investment patterns, and scenario-specific technology pathways. [End Step 7]

problem_statement: Li+ transport in organic–inorganic hybrid electrolytes is limited because Li+ must shed its organic solvation shell and cross particle/liquid interfaces before entering the inorganic phase. This interfacial step can offset the intrinsic conductivity advantage of inorganic fillers, making it difficult to design hybrid electrolytes with genuinely improved overall ion transport.
hypothesis: Applying suitably large Li+-conducting inorganic particles to a concentrated organic electrolyte addresses poor Li+ transport across hybrid electrolytes because reducing the number of particle/liquid interfacial crossings lowers the cumulative high-energy interfacial transport penalty, thereby increasing overall ionic conductivity.
problem_core: The fundamental bottleneck is the high-resistance, high-activation-energy Li+ transfer across particle/liquid interfaces in hybrid electrolytes, especially when small particles force repeated interfacial crossings.
problem_type_fine: particle/liquid interfacial Li+ transport barrier
failure_mode_or_limitation: slow Li+ transfer across inorganic particle/liquid interfaces due to desolvation and repeated interface crossing
intervention_or_solution: suspending large Li+-conducting LATP or Li6PS5Cl particles in a concentrated EC/LiTFSI electrolyte and analyzing impedance with a large-cell-constant setup
mechanism_or_rationale: Li+ transport in the hybrid medium proceeds through bulk liquid, bulk inorganic particles, and across particle/liquid interfaces; the latter process carries a larger resistance and activation energy because Li+ must transfer from its solvated liquid environment into the inorganic phase. Large particles can still enhance conductivity by providing conductive inorganic pathways while minimizing how often Li+ must cross these costly interfaces, whereas small particles increase interface-crossing frequency and therefore accumulate interfacial resistance that suppresses their transport contribution.
target_property: overall ionic conductivity and interfacial transport resistance
claimed_outcome: identification of large-particle hybrid electrolytes as more effective for conductivity enhancement and establishment of a practical impedance-based method to resolve bulk versus interfacial Li+ transport contributions
keywords: organic-inorganic hybrid electrolyte | Li+ transport | particle/liquid interface | desolvation barrier | interfacial resistance | ionic conductivity | LATP | Li6PS5Cl | high-concentration electrolyte | EC/LiTFSI | impedance spectroscopy | Nyquist semicircle | activation energy | particle size effect | Li+/Na+ exchange
keywords_compact: hybrid electrolyte | Li+ transport | interfacial resistance | LATP | Li6PS5Cl | impedance spectroscopy | particle size
reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] In hybrid organic–inorganic electrolytes, Li+ cannot move seamlessly between phases because it is solvated in the liquid and must adapt to the inorganic conduction environment before entering the particles. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] This phase-to-phase transfer creates a particle/liquid interfacial transport barrier, which is distinct from ion transport through the bulk liquid or the bulk inorganic conductor. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] Impedance measurements showing a high-frequency semicircle and a medium-frequency semicircle support separation of bulk transport from interfacial transport, with the medium-frequency process assigned to Li+ crossing particle/liquid interfaces. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] The observation that the medium-frequency resistance rises with particle loading and has a higher activation energy indicates that interfacial transfer is more energetically demanding than bulk conduction and can become the dominant penalty in hybrid electrolytes. [End Step 4]
[Begin Step 5] Because small particles shorten individual inorganic segments and force Li+ to encounter more interfaces over a given travel distance, they amplify the cumulative interfacial resistance and contribute less effectively to current transport. [End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] Therefore, using larger Li+-conducting particles is expected to better leverage inorganic conductivity while reducing repeated interfacial crossings, leading to higher net electrolyte conductivity and offering a rational design rule for hybrid electrolytes. [End Step 6]

problem_statement: LiFePO4 particles develop internal cracks during cycling because anisotropic Li insertion/extraction generates heterogeneous phase distributions and chemo-mechanical tensile stress. These cracks alter the Li transport pathway and can further accelerate stress buildup and crack propagation, undermining structural integrity and cycling reliability of the cathode particles.
hypothesis: Accounting for internal crack formation in LiFePO4 particles addresses unexplained transport heterogeneity and degradation because crack surfaces become new Li (de)insertion pathways and couple with local phase evolution to concentrate tensile stress at crack tips, thereby changing Li distribution, stress fields, and ultimately particle structural stability during cycling.

problem_type_fine: chemo-mechanical cracking in LFP particles

mechanism_or_rationale: In noncracked LiFePO4, Li extraction and insertion occur mainly from the original (010) side-edge surfaces, producing Li-rich/Li-poor phase heterogeneity that generates tensile stress. Once a crack forms, the newly created internal surface becomes an additional active Li transport interface, redirecting Li (de)insertion into the particle interior. This redistribution of concentration fields shifts stress localization to the cracked-core region and crack tip, promoting crack opening/closing and further propagation through a chemo-mechanical positive-feedback loop.
target_property: Li distribution pathway and internal chemo-mechanical stress field
claimed_outcome: mechanistic understanding of crack-accelerated degradation and redirected Li transport in LiFePO4 particles

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] In LiFePO4 cathode particles, lithiation and delithiation are spatially nonuniform rather than perfectly homogeneous, so local Li-rich and Li-poor domains form during cycling. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] In noncracked particles, Li exchange occurs primarily through the original (010) side-edge surfaces, which creates concentration gradients between the surface region and the core. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] These composition gradients generate anisotropic chemo-mechanical stress; during discharge, the Li-rich side-edge region and Li-poor core produce tensile stress that can nucleate internal cracks. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] After cracking, the crack surface acts as a new internal reaction interface, so Li (de)insertion is redirected away from only the external side edge and toward the cracked region. [End Step 4]
[Begin Step 5] This redirected Li pathway redistributes both concentration and stress fields, causing tensile stress localization at the cracked-core region and crack tip, which correlates with crack opening, closing, and propagation. [End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] Therefore, cracking is not just a passive consequence of cycling but part of a chemo-mechanically interactive feedback loop that accelerates structural degradation; operando STXM plus phase-field modeling directly support this mechanism. [End Step 6]

problem_statement: Urban wind prediction in dense built environments is limited by how building geometry is represented in CFD models, especially when the common LoD 1.2 representation enforces a single height per building footprint. This geometric simplification can distort local acceleration, separation, downwash, and turbulence patterns, which matters because wind assessments are used for pedestrian comfort, urban air applications, and UAV trajectory planning and risk forecasting.
hypothesis: Applying higher building geometric detail (LoD 2.2 rather than LoD 1.2) to RANS-based urban wind simulations addresses systematic misprediction of statistical wind risk because resolving multiple building heights, sloped roofs, and tower-like features changes canyon channelling, flow separation, and turbulence generation, thereby improving risk-map fidelity and associated wind-assessment outcomes.
problem_core: The paper seeks to overcome the bottleneck that simplified urban geometry representation causes biased prediction of mean wind and joint velocity–turbulence risk in complex urban CFD simulations.
problem_type_fine: geometry-induced wind prediction bias
component: urban built environment geometry representation in CFD domain
failure_mode_or_limitation: systematic under-representation of true building-height and roof-shape variability leading to biased wind speed and turbulence risk predictions
intervention_or_solution: Systematic comparison and use of higher geometric building level of detail, specifically LoD 2.2 instead of industry-standard LoD 1.2, combined with a joint exceedance risk-map framework based on velocity and turbulent kinetic energy across 1° wind-incidence simulations.
mechanism_or_rationale: LoD 2.2 preserves intra-footprint height differences, sloped roofs, and tall sub-features that LoD 1.2 smooths out into a single-height block. These geometric details alter local blockage, channelling, flow separation, recirculation, downwash, and turbulence production, so the resulting velocity and TKE fields—and especially their joint exceedance probability—change systematically. Because the proposed risk metric depends on both mean velocity and turbulence, it is more sensitive than averaged wind speed alone to geometry-induced flow-physics differences.
target_property: fidelity of joint exceedance probability risk maps based on wind speed and turbulent kinetic energy
claimed_outcome: More reliable identification of high-risk urban wind regions and improved cautionary guidance for UAV routing and pedestrian wind assessments, with LoD 2.2 avoiding the systematic under-prediction seen with LoD 1.2.
keywords: urban wind simulation | level of detail (LoD) | LoD 1.2 | LoD 2.2 | RANS CFD | building geometry representation | joint exceedance probability | risk map | turbulent kinetic energy | flow separation | urban canyon channelling | UAV trajectory planning | pedestrian wind comfort | urban morphology | geometric fidelity
keywords_compact: urban wind | LoD | RANS | risk map | TKE | UAV routing | pedestrian comfort
reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Urban planning, pedestrian safety, air-quality transport, and UAV operations all depend on accurate prediction of wind flow inside dense urban canopies. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Urban wind prediction is difficult because flow responds strongly to morphology through separation, recirculation, channelling, and turbulence, so the geometric representation of buildings becomes a first-order modelling choice. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] The standard LoD 1.2 representation assigns a single height to each building footprint and omits sloped roofs and tower-like sub-features, which under-represents the true height distribution and geometric heterogeneity. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] This simplification changes local blockage and corridor shape, which in turn modifies acceleration pathways, downwash regions, and turbulence generation compared with a more faithful LoD 2.2 geometry. [End Step 4]
[Begin Step 5] Because directionally averaged wind speed can appear only moderately different between LoDs, using velocity alone may mask geometry-induced errors in the more application-relevant statistical flow structure. [End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] A joint risk metric based on the probability that both normalized velocity and TKE exceed thresholds is therefore introduced to capture high-wind and high-turbulence regions relevant to UAV risk and related urban assessments. [End Step 6]
[Begin Step 7] Across two urban cases and 1° wind-direction sweeps, the data show that LoD 1.2 systematically under-predicts this joint risk relative to LoD 2.2, supporting the conclusion that higher geometric detail is needed for reliable urban wind risk forecasting. [End Step 7]

problem_statement: Conventional energy system modeling for deep decarbonization pathways mainly optimizes direct CO2 emissions and costs, while omitting broader life-cycle and indirect environmental burdens. problem_statement: Pristine 2D carbon materials such as graphene intrinsically have near-zero magnetic moment because their symmetric sp2 carbon lattice lacks the unpaired d/f electrons and sublattice imbalance needed for magnetic ordering. This limits their direct use in spintronic, memory, and related device applications, while excessive disorder or unsuitable modification can also degrade structural, thermal, and electronic performance.
hypothesis: Applying controlled structural disorder and/or targeted chemical modification to 2D carbon materials addresses their intrinsically poor magnetism because defects, edge states, dopants, and interfacial hybridization break lattice/pseudospin symmetry and create localized spin-polarized states or exchange interactions, thereby improving magnetic ordering and enabling spintronic-relevant functionality.
problem_core: The fundamental bottleneck is how to induce and tune robust magnetism in otherwise nonmagnetic 2D carbon lattices without relying on heavy conventional magnetic materials.
problem_type_fine: intrinsically poor magnetism in 2D carbon materials
component: 2D carbon lattice / basal plane and edge structure
failure_mode_or_limitation: absence of intrinsic magnetic ordering due to symmetric sp2 carbon network and zero net magnetic moment

mechanism_or_rationale: Disorder or chemical modification perturbs the ideal bipartite sp2 lattice, breaks pseudospin or sublattice symmetry, and generates localized electronic states with unpaired spins. Depending on the defect type, dopant chemistry, edge geometry, or interfacial hybridization, these local moments can couple through exchange, charge-transfer, or proximity interactions to produce paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, or spin-glass behavior. The same modifications also tune the local electronic structure and Fermi-level-dependent spin polarization, which is central to magnetic control in 2D carbon systems.
target_property: magnetic ordering and local spin polarization

problem_statement: Classical electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) represents electrochemical systems as linear time-invariant systems, so it is only valid for small-amplitude perturbations at steady operating points. This restricts the ability to interrogate batteries and other electrochemical interfaces during charging, discharging, aging, or interfacial evolution, where the voltage-current relation is nonlinear and the impedance changes with time. The limitation matters because important diagnostic information is then inaccessible, especially for state-of-health estimation, Li-plating detection, and adaptive charging control.
hypothesis: Applying multisine-based nonlinear and time-varying impedance analysis, particularly operando EIS/BLTVA estimation, to Li-ion battery measurements addresses the limitations of classical EIS because it separates linear, nonlinear, drift, and time-varying contributions in current-voltage data, thereby recovering impedance along operating trajectories and improving electrochemical diagnostics and charging-relevant monitoring.

problem_type_fine: nonlinear and nonstationary impedance characterization
failure_mode_or_limitation: classical EIS breakdown under nonlinearity, drift, and time-varying operating conditions
intervention_or_solution: Extend classical EIS with multisine excitations and advanced identification methods—Volterra-series/NLEIS, best linear approximation, time-varying impedance estimation, and operando EIS based on BLTVA with drift suppression.
mechanism_or_rationale: Multisine excitation distributes information across many harmonics simultaneously, enabling spectral detection of nonlinear distortions and nonstationary skirts that are not visible in classical single-point measurements. Volterra/BLA-based analysis captures the leading linear response in weakly nonlinear systems, while time-varying impedance and BLTVA formulations model impedance as a joint time-frequency quantity rather than a fixed transfer function. In operando EIS, basis-function expansion and explicit drift modeling separate evolving impedance, nonlinear distortion, and slow baseline signals, allowing low-frequency impedance to be estimated even during charging.
target_property: time-resolved and nonlinear impedance observability
claimed_outcome: extraction of informative impedance data beyond linearity and stationarity, enabling improved Li-ion battery monitoring, Li-plating detection, state-of-health diagnostics, and smart-charging control
novelty_axis: new diagnostic framework for operando impedance

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Electrochemical interfaces generate current-voltage responses that are inherently dynamic, but in practical systems such as Li-ion batteries these responses are also nonlinear and evolve with operating state, temperature, charging history, and aging. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Classical EIS assumes linearity and stationarity, so it only yields a local small-signal impedance around a fixed operating point and cannot directly describe batteries while charging/discharging or interfaces while they are changing. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] Because important degradation and control-relevant phenomena occur exactly under such evolving conditions, restricting measurements to steady-state small-signal conditions loses potentially useful information for SOH estimation, Li-plating detection, and adaptive charging. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] Using broadband odd random-phase multisine excitation allows many frequencies to be probed at once and makes nonlinearities and nonstationarities detectable in the voltage/current spectra through harmonic content and spectral skirts. [End Step 4]

[End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] Therefore, impedance can be estimated along operating trajectories rather than only at rest, providing richer diagnostic features such as time-varying charge-transfer resistance and nonclassical signatures that are proposed to improve battery health monitoring and smart charging performance. [End Step 6]

problem_statement: Na- and Li-layered cathodes that exploit anionic redox can deliver extra capacity, but their practical use is limited by voltage decay, sluggish kinetics, hysteresis, and partial irreversibility of oxygen oxidation. intervention_or_solution: magnetization-constrained DFT analysis to identify and control the Na-content/stacking regime favoring reversible collective distortion (reductive coupling) over oxygen disproportionation in P2-type Na-deficient Mn-based layered oxides
mechanism_or_rationale: Removing Na creates holes in localized oxygen non-bonding states, which are electronically unstable unless the system reorganizes. In P stacking, interlayer O-O pairing and symmetry-lowering enable Mn(d)-O(O) orbital mixing (reductive coupling), delocalizing/partially pairing oxygen holes and stabilizing a reversible collective distortion without band inversion. In O stacking or below a critical Na content, the structure instead disproportionates the oxygen network into strongly oxidized peroxo-like and weakly oxidized oxo-like species, driving Mg/Zn migration, increasing oxygen-release propensity, and causing hysteresis because discharge then follows a different electronic pathway.

claimed_outcome: identification of a critical composition and stacking criterion that predicts and can help suppress hysteresis, migration, oxygen release, and capacity fading while guiding design of more reversible Na (and Li) anionic-redox cathodes
novelty_axis: new mechanistic descriptor via magnetization-constrained DFT

keywords_compact: anionic redox | P2/O2 stacking | oxygen disproportionation | reductive coupling | magnetization-constrained DFT | voltage hysteresis | oxygen release
reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Na-deficient layered oxide cathodes can access extra capacity through oxygen redox, but deep oxidation often causes hysteresis, sluggish kinetics, and irreversibility that block practical deployment. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] In Na_xMg1/3Mn2/3O2, Na removal creates holes in narrow, localized oxygen lone-pair-derived states, producing an electronically unstable partially filled oxygen band if no further structural/electronic reorganization occurs. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] The material can stabilize these oxygen holes through two distinct pathways that depend strongly on stacking: P2 stacking allows homogeneous interlayer O-O pairing and a collective lattice distortion, whereas O2 stacking suppresses that geometry and instead favors oxygen-network disproportionation with cation migration. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] In the P2 pathway, symmetry lowering enables coupling between partially filled O-O sigma-star states and empty Mn(d)-derived antibonding states, producing a reductive-coupling mechanism that stabilizes the oxidized oxygen network while preserving a reversible reduction pathway. [End Step 4]
[Begin Step 5] In the O2 or low-Na pathway, oxygen holes localize unevenly into distinct oxygen sublattices, forming peroxo-like species and weakly oxidized oxo-like species; this disproportionation promotes Mg/Zn migration, raises oxygen-release risk, and causes band inversion that underlies voltage hysteresis. [End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] Because reductive coupling decreases total cell magnetization while disproportionation leaves closed-shell oxygen species largely nonmagnetic, the spin-dependent energy landscape provides a quantitative descriptor of which mechanism is lowest in energy at each Na content. [End Step 6]
[Begin Step 7] Therefore, determining the critical Na composition xc and favoring P-type stacking or designs that keep operation within the reductive-coupling regime should mitigate hysteresis, migration, oxygen loss, and capacity fading, enabling more reversible anionic-redox cathodes. [End Step 7]

problem_statement: Capacity fade in polycrystalline NMC622/natural graphite lithium-ion pouch cells depends strongly on state-of-charge range, C-rate, and temperature, but the relative roles of lithium inventory loss, impedance growth, and active mass loss remain difficult to separate and predict. problem_statement: Practical SERS applications are limited by the difficulty of fabricating plasmonic nanostructures that simultaneously provide dense, intense, and uniform hot spots over wafer-scale areas. intervention_or_solution: Combination of rapid thermal annealing, ALD deposition of a sacrificial ultrathin Al2O3 spacer, and controlled KOH etching to form wafer-scale Au NPs/nanogap/Au NPs structures with tunable 2-20 nm gaps

problem_statement: Accurate interpretation and application of electrochemical impedance spectroscopy for commercial Li-ion batteries are limited by poor metrological traceability, setup-dependent measurement uncertainty, and ambiguity in assigning spectral features to specific cell processes. hypothesis: Applying a metrology-informed, carefully controlled EIS workflow to commercial Li-ion cells addresses unreliable and ambiguous impedance analysis because traceable calibration, uncertainty-aware measurement design, validity checks, and complementary validation reduce artefacts and improve process attribution, thereby improving impedance reliability and diagnostic interpretation for state estimation and degradation analysis.

intervention_or_solution: state-of-the-art EIS methodology combining metrological traceability and calibration, controlled measurement setup and perturbation selection, Kramers-Kronig validity checks, physics-based/ECM interpretation, and postmortem or reconstructed-cell validation
mechanism_or_rationale: Traceable calibration and uncertainty-aware test fixtures reduce distortion from cables, contacts, and magnetic coupling, so the measured spectrum more faithfully represents the cell rather than the instrumentation. Careful control of perturbation amplitude, SOC, temperature, and rest conditions helps satisfy linearity, causality, and stationarity, making impedance features physically meaningful. Validation with Kramers-Kronig relations, harvested-electrode symmetric/half cells, and postmortem analyses helps deconvolute overlapping processes and link spectral changes to specific interfacial, transport, or degradation phenomena.

claimed_outcome: more reliable EIS-based diagnosis, state estimation, degradation analysis, and performance assessment of commercial LIBs

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Commercial Li-ion cells exhibit complex impedance contributions from ohmic, interfacial, and diffusional processes, and these contributions strongly affect voltage loss, rate capability, efficiency, capacity, and ageing diagnostics. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] Because commercial cells are low-impedance, two-electrode systems, their EIS spectra are especially sensitive to measurement artefacts from fixtures, cables, contacts, shielding limitations, and insufficient traceability in the relevant low-frequency, below-0.1-ohm range. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] Even if spectra are measured, overlapping time constants from anode, cathode, SEI, and contact processes can merge into similar arcs, making feature attribution ambiguous and weakening links between impedance and physical degradation or state variables. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] Therefore, the design criterion is not merely to collect spectra, but to obtain impedance data under controlled perturbation amplitude, temperature, SOC, and geometry with calibration and uncertainty handling that make the measurement physically valid and repeatable. [End Step 4]
[Begin Step 5] Metrological practices such as traceable calibration, four-terminal-pair concepts where possible, and OSL compensation act by subtracting fixture and short-path parasitics and reducing electromagnetic coupling errors, so the recorded response better reflects the DUT itself. [End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] Mathematical validation via Kramers-Kronig relations and experimental validation via postmortem analysis, three-electrode/symmetric reconstructed cells, and complementary microscopy/spectroscopy link specific impedance changes to actual electrode, SEI, separator, electrolyte, or structural changes. [End Step 6]
[Begin Step 7] Consequently, a combined metrology-measurement-validation framework is proposed to improve confidence in EIS-derived interpretation, enabling more robust state estimation, ageing diagnosis, and mechanistic understanding of commercial LIB behaviour. [End Step 7]

problem_statement: Magnetic-field compression during encounters of independently advected plasma structures is observed across astrophysical systems, yet the measured compression factor is typically only a few despite the much larger compression expected when embedded fields are compressed with matter. hypothesis: Bringing two counter-propagating plasma plumes carrying parallel magnetic fields into controlled interaction addresses the unresolved origin of limited magnetic-field compression because the encounter builds magnetic pressure and induces flow-driven electric fields that decelerate and redirect inflows, thereby limiting further field accumulation and explaining the observed saturated compression ratio.

problem_type_fine: saturated magnetic-field compression during plasma-plume interaction
component: interaction zone between two magnetized plasma plumes
failure_mode_or_limitation: magnetic-field compression saturates at relatively low ratios because inflows are decelerated and diverted at the compressed sheet
intervention_or_solution: laboratory generation of two counter-propagating laser-produced plasma plumes with parallel toroidal magnetic fields, combined with proton radiography and matched 3D hybrid simulations
mechanism_or_rationale: When the two frozen-in magnetic structures encounter one another, magnetic flux accumulates into a compressed sheet and the associated magnetic-pressure gradient slows the incoming plasma. Simultaneously, flow penetration into the opposing field generates a Vinflow × B electric field, and the resulting electric-field structure drives transverse and sheet-aligned redirection of the inflows via E × B drift. These coupled effects prevent continued head-on plasma advection into the sheet, so magnetic compression saturates rather than growing to extreme values.

claimed_outcome: direct evidence and mechanistic explanation for robust, modest magnetic-field compression during collisions of parallel magnetized plasma structures, with compression saturating at order-few to order-tens rather than thousands
novelty_axis: new mechanistic insight via experiment-simulation matching

keywords_compact: magnetic compression | plasma-plume collision | magnetic pressure | Vinflow x B field | E x B drift | hybrid PIC | proton radiography
reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Observations in space and astrophysical plasmas show that collisions between independent magnetized structures produce only limited magnetic-field compression, creating a contradiction with the much larger compression expected when matter carrying embedded field is compressed globally. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] To isolate the physics of this contradiction, the study recreates two independently generated, parallel-oriented magnetic structures using counter-propagating laser-driven plasma plumes whose fields are frozen into the expanding plasma. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] Proton radiography reveals a localized magnetic-field buildup and density pile-up between the plumes, showing that the field does compress at the interaction zone but not without bound. [End Step 3]

[End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] Because redirected inflow can no longer keep piling magnetic flux into the interaction zone, the compressed field reaches a robust saturation level, explaining why the magnetic compression ratio remains modest in both the laboratory system and analogous astrophysical encounters. [End Step 6]

problem_statement: Lithium-ion batteries suffer poor capacity retention at moderately elevated temperatures, where impedance growth and loss of cyclable lithium are linked to instability of the anode solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). A key limitation is the incomplete mechanistic understanding of how major SEI carbonate species evolve and decompose in the presence of LiPF6-containing electrolyte, which hinders accurate modeling of ion transport and strategies to improve calendar life.
hypothesis: Investigating the thermal reaction of representative SEI carbonates (Li2CO3, LMC, and LEDC) with LiPF6 in DMC addresses the unclear origin of SEI instability because LiPF6-derived reactive phosphorus/fluorine species are proposed to drive carbonate decomposition, transesterification, and fluorophosphate formation, thereby clarifying SEI compositional evolution and its impact on interfacial stability in lithium-ion batteries.

failure_mode_or_limitation: thermal instability and decomposition of SEI carbonate species in the presence of LiPF6 electrolyte
intervention_or_solution: Systematic thermal-aging study of Li2CO3, lithium methyl carbonate (LMC), and lithium ethylene dicarbonate (LEDC) in LiPF6/DMC using combined NMR, GC-MS, IR-ATR, and XPS analysis.
mechanism_or_rationale: The study indicates that LiPF6 strongly destabilizes SEI lithium carbonates that are otherwise stable in DMC alone. For Li2CO3, reaction with LiPF6 yields LiF, CO2, and soluble F2PO2Li, while for alkyl carbonates LMC and LEDC the alkoxy substituents enable PF5/LiPF6-mediated transesterification, etherification, and related decomposition pathways that generate ethers, phosphates, and fluorophosphates in addition to LiF and CO2. This mechanistic mapping explains how the SEI chemically evolves during thermal aging and why fluorine-rich, phosphorus-poor interphases can form.
target_property: SEI compositional stability and evolution under thermal aging
claimed_outcome: Direct identification of LiPF6-mediated SEI decomposition pathways, providing insight into anode SEI evolution and factors contributing to calendar-life degradation.

[Begin Step 2] The anode SEI initially contains Li2CO3, LMC, and LEDC, but their long-term evolution in LiPF6-based electrolyte is insufficiently understood, limiting mechanistic interpretation of interfacial aging and ion transport. [End Step 2]

problem_statement: Membrane electrolysis processes are often limited by the need to simultaneously maintain low ohmic resistance, high ion selectivity, chemical stability, and mechanical robustness under harsh electrochemical conditions. intervention_or_solution: use of chemically stable ion-selective membranes, especially perfluorinated sulfonated or bilayer sulfonic/carboxylic membranes, integrated in zero-gap membrane electrolysis cell designs
mechanism_or_rationale: The membrane physically separates anolyte and catholyte while permitting preferential counter-ion transport, which suppresses undesired reactions of products or intermediates at the opposite electrode and increases product purity. When implemented in a zero-gap configuration, the membrane also shortens the interelectrode distance and reduces electrolyte-phase ohmic drop and gas void effects. problem_statement: Thermal runaway in lithium-ion cells is often initiated by internal short circuits (ISCs), but the resistance of an ISC during nail penetration is poorly understood because conventional analyses usually assume a constant or full-penetration resistance. mechanism_or_rationale: The method isolates the penetrated region and uses a four-tab configuration so that ISC current and local cell voltage can be measured directly and converted to instantaneous ISC resistance. claimed_outcome: More accurate identification of transient high-risk ISC states, improved interpretation of thermal-runaway hazard during nail penetration, and mechanistic guidance for designing more robust abuse-tolerant Li-ion cells.

problem_statement: Strain engineering is widely pursued to enhance oxide-ion conduction in electrochemical oxide thin films, but the role of plastic strain associated with dislocations remains unclear and experimentally contradictory. intervention_or_solution: atomistic simulation and DFT-guided mechanistic analysis of a 1/2<110>{100} edge dislocation in reduced and trivalent-doped CeO2
mechanism_or_rationale: The edge-dislocation strain field elastically attracts or repels dopant cations depending on their size mismatch with Ce4+, producing local dopant enrichment and depletion zones. Oxygen vacancies then follow the dopant distribution through electrostatic attraction rather than behaving as an intrinsically fast pipe-diffusion species. The resulting high-defect-density regions suffer from strong dopant-vacancy and vacancy-vacancy association, while depleted regions lack mobile charge carriers, so both effects reduce vacancy mobility and suppress oxide-ion transport along and across the dislocation.

claimed_outcome: edge dislocations are shown to be detrimental rather than beneficial to oxide-ion conduction, leading to reduced diffusivity and no pipe-diffusion enhancement
novelty_axis: new mechanistic insight into dislocation-defect coupling

reasoning_process:
[Begin Step 1] Strained oxide thin films are often expected to show enhanced ionic transport, but these systems also contain high dislocation densities, and prior literature gives contradictory interpretations of whether dislocations help conduction. [End Step 1]
[Begin Step 2] In vacancy-mediated ceria, oxygen transport depends sensitively on the spatial distribution and interactions of dopants, reduced cations, and oxygen vacancies, so a dislocation could alter transport by changing local defect chemistry rather than by acting as an open diffusion pipe. [End Step 2]
[Begin Step 3] Atomistic simulations of a single 1/2<110>{100} edge dislocation show that elastic energy minimization drives dopant cations to segregate into tensile or compressive regions depending on dopant size relative to Ce4+, creating corresponding enrichment and depletion zones. [End Step 3]
[Begin Step 4] Oxygen vacancies are then redistributed mainly by electrostatic attraction to the segregated trivalent cations, so vacancy enrichment/depletion mirrors dopant segregation more strongly than vacancy-dislocation interaction alone. [End Step 4]
[Begin Step 5] In enrichment zones, locally excessive dopant and vacancy concentrations increase associative defect interactions and migration barriers, whereas in depletion zones the scarcity of oxygen vacancies lowers the concentration of mobile carriers; thus both regions hinder transport. [End Step 5]
[Begin Step 6] Consequently, molecular dynamics and supporting DFT+U calculations indicate that edge dislocations in doped/reduced ceria do not provide fast pipe diffusion and instead reduce local oxide-ion diffusivity, implying that dislocations can be detrimental to conductivity in similarly defect-rich oxides. [End Step 6]
